accuracy.evidence: Checked against Mischel, Ebbesen and Zeiss (1972, J Pers Soc Psychol) and Mischel, Shoda and Rodriguez (1989, Science): covered or absent rewards and self-distraction (singing, playing) lengthened waiting, attending to the reward shortened it. The reliability point is from Kidd, Palmeri and Aslin (2013, Cognition), and the caution about long-term prediction from Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018, Psychological Science). The get-help-now cards follow NSPCC and PSHE Association safeguarding guidance that hurt, illness or being hurt by someone are told to a trusted adult at once.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets what children (and adults) get wrong about waiting: that looking at the treat helps you stay ready (step 3 prediction, challenge 'stare', m8), that asking again makes it come sooner (Keep asking card, challenge 'nag', m5), that grabbing or shouting gets a turn faster (step 4 scenes, challenge 'grab', p3), that patience means waiting even when hurt or unsafe (step 5 prediction, challenge 'hurt', m6, p5), and that waiting is meant to feel fun (challenge 'fun').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpatient is about delaying a reward: a one-now-or-two-later choice with a five-tap sand timer, dragging a cup over the biscuit and a tablet into a drawer while a want-meter drops, a grid of eight strategy cards, three asking scenes, and a can-wait versus get-help-now sort. flagwait (ages 3–4) is turn-taking in a slide line and counting swings. Gate similarity is under 30% to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner experiences the trade-off directly (eating now gives 1, finishing the timer gives 2), sees the want-meter fall only when the treat is hidden, gets a reason each time an unhelpful trick or rude request is chosen, and finds the limit of patience by sorting a bleeding knee and feeling sick into get help now. Each completion line names the strategy just used.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option: eat it now gives more (step 1, disproved by 2 biscuits after the timer), staring at the cake helps (step 3, disproved because Stare at the treat is rejected with the reason), and a bad tummy ache should be waited out quietly (step 5, disproved by the get-help-now box). The reveal line after each task confirms the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Each wrong option has its own message: stare (keeps your mind on it), hold (very hard to wait), grab (can hurt, ask kindly), nag (does not make it sooner), hurt (do not wait, tell a grown-up), cry (feelings OK, find something to do), fun (waiting can be hard and that is OK) and soon (waiting means later). Six questions rotate.

readability.evidence: Kid text is FK grade 0.4 against the family target of 5; every sentence is short and concrete (One biscuit now, or two biscuits after the timer?). Lab card texts are 2 to 7 words. Adult text is FK 7.1 against a 10 target and uses the terms delayed gratification, self-regulation and impulse control.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea: what patience is, why waiting can pay, which tricks help, how to ask and when not to wait. Every lab message is a task or a reason for that specific choice (Licking the treat: Tasting it makes it very hard to stop). No banned phrases pass the content gate.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and dark screenshots of all 6 steps: the trick grid is 2 columns of large cards on the phone, scene options are full-width cards, the cup and tablet are separate drag targets about 70 px wide, and every action has a big button under the canvas. The sand timer outline was changed to the theme text colour after the dark screenshot showed it was too faint.

accessibility.evidence: The walkthrough gate ran every step with Show me on desktop and iPhone and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme. All drags (cup, tablet, sort card) have button equivalents, the timer can be advanced by its button, and the canvas aria-label is updated with every message.
